shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example recomputing at a quantity a child names and showing the ranking hold.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

visual_behaviour.never: Do not highlight either offer while a prediction is still open or before both rates are computed, and never draw unequal segments. Unequal segments would produce a number that is not a rate.
visual_behaviour.scene: Two horizontal tape bars, one per offer, labelled with quantity and price. Split segments are drawn with equal widths and tick separators, and the unit rate sits under each bar. The better offer takes the primary accent once the comparison is made.
visual_behaviour.layout: Bars stacked in the main panel with their rates beneath and the comparison panel under both. On a 390 px frame the bars keep full width and segments never fall below 12 px.
readouts: Each offer's quantity and price, always on screen
Each unit rate, once computed, as an exact fraction with any rounding rule stated
The ranking and the quantity it was checked at
animations: Split: segment separators appear left to right over 220 ms with equal spacing, so equality is seen being imposed.
Rate landing: the unit rate writes itself under the bar as the last segment lands, so the rate arrives from the split.
Quantity change: both bars restretch to the new quantity while the ranking indicator holds still, which is the invariance made watchable.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Bar length is proportional to quantity so the two offers are visually comparable; segments never fall below 12 px, and above 24 segments the bar shows a grouped count instead.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The split into equal parts has to be watched before the division is written, or the unit rate is a formula rather than the value of one of the pieces the bar was actually cut into

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to break the comparison the class arrives with. Both totals are on screen, 60 and 88, and the bigger total belongs to the offer that is actually the better buy - which the heights already say and the numbers do not. Do not compute a rate here and do not say the words unit rate: the beat's whole work is making 'which costs less in total' visibly the wrong question.

Beat 2 is the unitary method happening rather than being stated. Each bar divides into as many equal parts as it has items, the FIRST part lights up, and the cost of one item writes itself underneath - so the rate arrives out of the cutting rather than out of a formula. Count PARTS aloud, never separators: four parts show three lines between them, and counting the lines is the off-by-one this beat exists to pre-empt.

Beat 3 turns the observation into the reason a rate is the right thing to compare at all. Both offers are recosted at 40, which draws both bars at the SAME width, so only the heights are left to decide and the ranking cannot move. Say what stayed the same only AFTER both totals have landed, and read every number off the tool.
media.generation_prompt: Unit Rate Finder: two offers as tape bars split into equal segments, where the cheaper is highlighted only after both unit rates have been computed
media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read both offers and predict which is the better value before you calculate anything. 2. Split each bar into equal parts and read the cost of one item under each. 3. Type each unit rate and let the tool check it against the exact fraction. 4. Press Compare and see which offer is better value. 5. Change the quantity for both offers and check whether the ranking moves. 6. Switch to items per rupee and say which number is now the larger one. 7. Say why you chose the unit you compared in. 8. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

content.text:
Form a pair. Collect 12 countable objects or counters (it can be coins, seeds, or pebbles). Now, share them between the two of you in different ways.
If you divide them equally, what is the ratio of the number of counters with each of you? Each of you will get 6 counters. So, the ratio is 6 : 6, or 1 : 1 in its simplest form.
Now let us not share equally. If your partner gets 5 counters, how many objects will you get? What is the ratio of the counters? The ratio of the counters of your partner to yours is 5 : 7.
Now, if you want to share the counters between the two of you in the ratio of 3 : 1, how many counters would each of you get?
So, your partner gets 9 counters in total and you get 3 counters.
Now, if you want to share 42 counters between the two of you in the ratio of 4 : 3, how will you do it? Using the same procedure would take a long time! There is a simpler way to share the whole with parts in a specified ratio.
You need to divide 42 into groups such that your partner gets 4 groups and you get 3 groups.
If your partner gets 4 groups and you get 3 groups, the total number of groups is 7. So, the size of each group is 42 ÷ 7 = 6.
Multiplying the number of groups by the size of each group, your partner gets 24 counters and you get 18 counters, when you share 42 counters in the ratio of 4 : 3.

3. A faster way: one round uses 3 + 1 = 4 counters, so 12 makes 12 ÷ 4 = 3 rounds.

Worked example: Share 12 counters in the ratio 3 : 1, and then 42 counters in the ratio 4 : 3.
1. 12 in 3 : 1: one round takes 3 + 1 = 4 counters, and 12 ÷ 4 = 3 rounds.
2. Partner: 3 × 3 = 9; you: 1 × 3 = 3.
3. 42 in 4 : 3: there are 4 + 3 = 7 groups, each of 42 ÷ 7 = 6.
4. Partner: 4 × 6 = 24; you: 3 × 6 = 18. Check: 24 + 18 = 42.
Answer: 12 shared 3 : 1 gives 9 and 3; 42 shared 4 : 3 gives 24 and 18

concepts.concept_name: The general rule: sharing a profit

content.text:
In general, when we want to divide a quantity, say x, in the ratio m : n, we do the following:
We need to split x into groups such that it can be divided into two parts where the first part has m groups and the second part has n groups.
But what is the size of each group? This can be found out by dividing x by the number of groups. The number of groups are m + n.
Thus, if we want to divide a quantity x in the ratio of m : n, then the parts will be m × x/(m + n) and n × x/(m + n).
Prashanti and Bhuvan started a food cart business near their school. Prashanti invested ₹75,000 and Bhuvan invested ₹25,000. At the end of the first month, they gained a profit of ₹4,000. They decided that they would share the profit in the same ratio as that of their investment. What is each person's share of the profit?
The ratio of their investment is 75000 : 25000. Reducing this ratio to its simplest form, we get 3 : 1.
3 + 1 is 4 and dividing the profit of 4000 by 4, we get 1000.
So, Prashanti would get ₹3,000 and Bhuvan would get ₹1,000 of the profit.

content.text:
Worked example: Prashanti invests ₹75000 and Bhuvan ₹25000. They share a profit of ₹4000 in the ratio of their investments. What does each get?
1. Ratio of investments: 75000 : 25000; the HCF is 25000, so it is 3 : 1.
2. Number of groups: 3 + 1 = 4; each group is 4000 ÷ 4 = 1000.
3. Prashanti: 3 × 1000 = 3000; Bhuvan: 1 × 1000 = 1000.
4. Check: 3000 + 1000 = 4000, and 3000 : 1000 is 3 : 1.
Answer: Prashanti gets ₹3000 and Bhuvan gets ₹1000

content.text:
A mixture of 40 kg contains sand and cement in the ratio of 3 : 1. How much cement should be added to the mixture to make the ratio of sand to cement 5 : 2?
The ratio is 3 : 1 and the total weight is 40 kg. So, the weight of sand is 3/(3 + 1) × 40 = 30 kg. The weight of cement is 1/(3 + 1) × 40 = 10 kg.
The weight of sand is the same in the new mixture. It remains 30. But the new ratio of sand to cement is 5 : 2. So the question is, 5 : 2 :: 30 : ?
The new mixture should have 12 kg of cement if the ratio of sand to cement is to be 5 : 2.
There is 10 kg of cement already. So, we need to add 2 kg of cement to the original mixture.

media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.7 Proportional Reasoning-1, the section 'Sharing, but Not Equally'. The class has met ratio, terms, equal parts and the unitary method, and has NOT met percentage-of or scale factor by name. The tool is read where a ratio is used to SPLIT rather than to compare, and the equal part is the object the whole method rests on. Notation follows the textbook: the colon with spaces (2 : 3), rupees written as ₹1200, and the part value given as the fraction x/(m+n) rather than a decimal.

overview.goal: The student divides an amount in a stated ratio using equal parts and explains why the total number of parts matters.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A single horizontal bar across the working ground, labelled with its total and waiting to be divided. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class shares an amount in a two term ratio by cutting it into two pieces, and the bar is asked whether the pieces add back up.
overview.concept: To divide a total in a given ratio, first split it into as many equal parts as the ratio terms add to, then give each share its number of parts. The total number of parts is the sum of the terms, not the number of terms, which is why a two term ratio rarely means splitting into two.
overview.purpose: The student divides an amount in a stated ratio using equal parts and explains why the total number of parts matters.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Bar across the main panel with the part value beneath and the share readouts under that. The wrong route bar appears below when shown. On a 390 px frame the bar keeps full width and the segments never fall below 12 px. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not compute any share while a prediction is still open, and never draw parts of unequal length in the correct route. Unequal parts would make the method meaningless.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Every part must be the same size, or the shares would not be in the stated ratio. If one share is m parts and the other is n, then together they are m plus n parts, and those parts make up the whole. So the part value is the total divided by m plus n, and each share follows. Splitting into two parts named 2 and 3 makes parts of different sizes, which is why the shares then fail to add to the total. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the total bar whole and asks how many equal parts are needed to share it in the ratio 2 to 3. Beat 2 splits it into five equal parts and groups them 2 and 3, with each share computed from the part value. Beat 3 runs the wrong route, splitting into two parts named 2 and 3, and the shares fail to add to the total. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setParts, groupParts, showWrongRoute and say.
whatYouLearned: Sharing in the ratio m to n needs m plus n equal parts

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the whole bar with its total labelled, the ratio stated and no parts drawn, and ask the class to say out loud how many equal parts are needed first. Commit the class number on the prediction pad. Target: the whole bar. Never split the bar before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Split the bar into the parts the ratio calls for and drag the group divider so the two groups match the two terms. Targets: the part count and the group divider. Read the part value and both shares from the tool's own readouts and never from this plan. Call 3. Turn on the wrong route so a second bar is split into as many pieces as there are terms, and point at the shortfall as the two shares are summed. Targets: the wrong route bar and the shortfall readout. Never say what the wrong route gets wrong before the sum has stopped short.

hunts: ADD THEM BACK: try the wrong route on three totals and record how far the shares land from the bar.
ZERO TERM: share an amount in a ratio with a zero in it and say why the bar still fills.
EXACT FRACTION: find a total the part count does not divide, and check the two shares still add up.
WORK BACKWARDS: hide the total, give a classmate one share and the ratio, and see if they can recover it.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each share is a whole number of parts, so all the parts have to be the same size for the ratio to hold
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The bar is cut into as many equal parts as the terms add to, never into as many parts as there are terms
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The sum of the terms is a count of parts, which is why a two term ratio rarely means cutting in two

observationsAndConclusions.why: Unequal pieces named 2 and 3 do not carry the part value, so the shares no longer make up the whole
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The wrong route leaves the running total stopping short of the end of the bar
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Shares that fail to add back to the total prove the part count was wrong, without any need to be told

observationsAndConclusions.why: Rounding each share would change their sum, so the total would no longer be recovered
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A total the part count does not divide is kept as an exact fraction rather than rounded
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: An awkward part value is not an impossible share; it is a share that must be kept exact

media.description: A single horizontal bar stands on the working ground with its total written above it and the ratio written at its far end. The bar is cut into equal segments generated from one division, so every part is identical to the pixel, and a heavier divider groups those parts into the shares the ratio names, each group tinted in its own accent with its value printed beneath it and its part count printed above. The value of one part sits under the middle of the bar, kept as a stacked fraction whenever the total does not divide evenly, and the add-back line closes the share-out the way an Indian classroom does. Turning on the wrong route draws a second bar beneath, cut into as many pieces as there are names in the ratio, with the run those pieces would actually demand drawn at the SAME unit from the SAME origin so it is seen bursting past the bar's own end, the overshoot printed in rupees. Three-term ratios run through the identical rule with the sum of all three terms as the part count, and a reverse problem leaves the total slot reading ? with the given share ringed across exactly its own segments, so the forward routine has nothing to divide and the part value has to be recovered first.

concept.notation: Sharing in the ratio m to n means m parts to one share and n to the other, out of m plus n equal parts in total.
concept.statement: To divide a total in a given ratio, first split it into as many equal parts as the ratio terms add to, then give each share its number of parts. The total number of parts is the sum of the terms, not the number of terms, which is why a two term ratio rarely means splitting into two.
prerequisites: reading a ratio as a comparison of parts
misconceptions: Dividing by the number of ratio terms rather than by the sum of the terms.
Sharing by the difference between the terms.
concept.why_it_is_true: Every part must be the same size, or the shares would not be in the stated ratio. If one share is m parts and the other is n, then together they are m plus n parts, and those parts make up the whole. So the part value is the total divided by m plus n, and each share follows. Splitting into two parts named 2 and 3 makes parts of different sizes, which is why the shares then fail to add to the total.
worked_numbers: 1200 in the ratio 2 to 3 needs 5 equal parts of 240, giving 480 and 720.
The wrong route splits into two parts and the shares do not add to 1200.
1200 in the ratio 1 to 2 to 3 needs 6 parts of 200, giving 200, 400 and 600.

answer_key.ground_truth: partValue(total, terms) = total divided by the sum of the terms, exactly. shares(total, terms) = each term times the part value. totalFromShare(share, term, terms) = share divided by term times the sum of the terms.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the part COUNT the thing the class looks at, before any value is computed. Two names in the ratio, five parts on the bar: that gap is the whole lesson, and it is on screen as a picture before it is anything else. Ask the class for the count out loud before you land the beat.

Beat 2 is the mechanism. Both shares are counts of the SAME part, so their total is 5 parts, which is the whole bar, the add-back line is not a check bolted on afterwards, it is the reason the method works. Point at the two groups and let the class say 2 parts and 3 parts before you read the rupees.

Beat 3 runs the shortcut and lets the arithmetic refuse it. Cutting into 2 pieces makes each piece ₹600, and 2 of them plus 3 of them demands ₹3000 from a bar worth ₹1200, the strip is drawn at the same unit from the same origin, so it visibly bursts past the bar's end. Never say what is wrong with the route before the strip has crossed the line.

media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read the total on the bar and the ratio you are sharing it in. 2. Predict how many equal parts the bar has to be cut into. 3. Set the part count and read the value of one part. 4. Drag the group divider until the groups match the terms of the ratio. 5. Type each share and check it against the value the part count gives. 6. Add the shares together and check that they come back to the total. 7. Turn on the wrong route and read the shortfall it leaves. 8. Try a reverse problem: from one share and the ratio, recover the total. 9. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

source_video_walkthrough.placement: after the concept's text
items: Share 12 counters in the ratio 3 : 1, and then 42 counters i

source: Share 12 counters in the ratio 3 : 1, and then 42 counters i
video_script.why: The child has used ratios to compare; now the child splits a whole into two parts that keep a given ratio.
video_script.substitution: Add the terms, divide the whole by that sum, then multiply each term by the result.
video_script.anchor: a row of twelve counters shared between you and your partner, then forty two counters shared the same way
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko divides forty two by three alone and gets fourteen, so the other share is twenty eight. Fourteen to twenty eight is one to two, not four to three; the whole must be divided by the sum of the terms, seven.
video_script.payoff_line: Twelve counters shared three to one give nine and three

final_answer.spoken: nine and three, and twenty four and eighteen

never_show: 14 and 28 marked as right
maths_rules: 12 counters in 3 : 1: one round = 3 + 1 = 4 counters; rounds = 12 / 4 = 3
42 counters in 4 : 3: groups = 4 + 3 = 7; one group = 42 / 7 = 6
partner 4 x 6 = 24; you 3 x 6 = 18; 24 + 18 = 42; 24 : 18 = 4 : 3 (divide both by 6)
video_script.design: One idea: add the terms, find one group, multiply each term. Wrong idea: divide the whole by one term only. The counters stay on the stage and the working goes on the board.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students share 12 counters in the ratio 3 : 1 by taking turns, then share 42 counters in the ratio 4 : 3 by finding the number of groups and the size of each group.
Students state the two parts for sharing x in the ratio m : n, and use them to share a profit in the ratio of the investments.
Students find the sand and cement in a 40 kg mixture in the ratio 3 : 1, keep the sand fixed and find how much cement to add to make the ratio 5 : 2.
Students split a bar into m + n equal groups, give m groups and n groups to the two parts, and solve sharing problems with money, solutions, paint, food, a crane's body and a coin's metals.

content.text:
Figure it Out (ratio sharing, question 2): In a science lab, acid and water are mixed in the ratio of 1 : 5 to make a solution. In a bottle that has 240 mL of the solution, how much acid and water does the solution contain?
1. Groups: 1 + 5 = 6.
2. One group: 240 ÷ 6 = 40 mL.
3. Acid: 1 × 40 = 40 mL; water: 5 × 40 = 200 mL.
Answer: 40 mL of acid and 200 mL of water

content.text:
Figure it Out (ratio sharing, question 3): Blue and yellow paints are mixed in the ratio of 3 : 5 to produce green paint. To produce 40 mL of green paint, how much of these two colours are needed? To make the paint a lighter shade of green, I added 20 mL of yellow to the mixture. What is the new ratio of blue and yellow in the paint?
1. Groups: 3 + 5 = 8; one group: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 mL.
2. Blue: 3 × 5 = 15 mL; yellow: 5 × 5 = 25 mL.
3. After adding yellow: 25 + 20 = 45 mL of yellow.
4. New ratio 15 : 45; the HCF is 15, so it is 1 : 3.
Answer: 15 mL of blue and 25 mL of yellow; the new ratio is 1 : 3

Figure it Out (ratio sharing, question 4): To make soft idlis, you need to mix rice and urad dal in the ratio of 2 : 1. If you need 6 cups of this mixture to make idlis tomorrow morning, how many cups of rice and urad dal will you need?

3. Rice: 2 × 2 = 4 cups; urad dal: 1 × 2 = 2 cups.

content.text:
Figure it Out (ratio sharing, question 5): I have one bucket of orange paint that I made by mixing red and yellow paints in the ratio of 3 : 5. I added another bucket of yellow paint to this mixture. What is the ratio of red paint to yellow paint in the new mixture?
1. Take both buckets to hold the same amount, and split one bucket into 3 + 5 = 8 equal groups.
2. The orange bucket has 3 groups of red and 5 groups of yellow.
3. A full bucket of yellow adds 8 more groups of yellow: 5 + 8 = 13.
4. Red to yellow is now 3 : 13.
Answer: 3 : 13 (taking both buckets to hold the same amount)

Figure it Out (unit conversions, question 4): A crane of height 155 cm has its neck and the rest of its body in the ratio 4 : 6. For your height, if your neck and the rest of the body also had this ratio, how tall would your neck be?
1. Groups: 4 + 6 = 10; the neck takes 4 of every 10 parts of the height.
2. For the crane: 4 ÷ 10 × 155 = 62 cm of neck.
3. For your height, say 150 cm: 4 ÷ 10 × 150 = 60 cm.
4. So your neck would be 4/10 of your height.
Answer: 4/10 of your height, for example 60 cm for a height of 150 cm (the crane's neck is 62 cm)

content.text:
Figure it Out (unit conversions, question 12): The ₹10 coin is an alloy of copper and nickel called cupro-nickel. Copper and nickel are mixed in a 3 : 1 ratio to get this alloy. The mass of the coin is 7.74 grams. If the cost of copper is ₹906 per kg and the cost of nickel is ₹1341 per kg, what is the cost of these metals in a ₹10 coin?
1. Groups: 3 + 1 = 4. Copper: 7.74 × 3 ÷ 4 = 5.805 g; nickel: 7.74 ÷ 4 = 1.935 g.
2. Same units: 1 kg is 1000 g. Copper cost: 906 × 5.805 ÷ 1000 ≈ 5.26 rupees.
3. Nickel cost: 1341 × 1.935 ÷ 1000 ≈ 2.59 rupees.
4. Total: 5.26 + 2.59 = 7.85 rupees.
Answer: About ₹7.85 (about ₹5.26 of copper and ₹2.59 of nickel)

content.text:
We have noticed earlier that solving problems with proportionality often requires us to convert units from one system to another. Here are a few important unit conversions for your reference.
Length: 1 metre = 3.281 feet.
Area: 1 square metre = 10.764 square feet; 1 acre = 43,560 square feet; 1 hectare = 10,000 square metres; 1 hectare = 2.471 acres.
Volume: 1 millilitre (mL) = 1 cubic centimetre (cc); 1 litre = 1,000 mL or 1,000 cc.

content.text:
Worked example: A field is 2 hectares. How many acres is it? How many square metres?
1. 1 hectare is 2.471 acres, so 1 : 2.471 :: 2 : x.
2. 2 × 2.471 = 4.942 acres.
3. 1 hectare is 10000 square metres, so 2 × 10000 = 20000 square metres.
Answer: 4.942 acres, which is 20000 square metres

content.text:
Temperature conversion between Fahrenheit and Celsius is a bit more complicated.
0 °C = 32 °F, and Fahrenheit = 9/5 × Celsius + 32 and Celsius = 5/9 × (Fahrenheit − 32).
For example, 25 °C is 77 °F.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if 0 °C is 32 °F, is 50 °C equal to 64 °F?
2. The formula multiplies and then adds 32, so doubling Celsius does not double Fahrenheit.
3. Celsius to Fahrenheit: multiply by 9/5, then add 32.
4. Fahrenheit to Celsius: subtract 32 first, then multiply by 5/9.

content.text:
Worked example: Convert 25 °C to Fahrenheit, and convert the answer back to Celsius.
1. 9/5 × 25 = 45.
2. 45 + 32 = 77, so 25 °C is 77 °F.
3. Back: 77 − 32 = 45.
4. 5/9 × 45 = 25, so 77 °F is 25 °C.
Answer: 25 °C is 77 °F

content.text:
Figure it Out (unit conversions, question 8): It is good farming practice to apply 10 tonnes of cow manure for 1 acre of land. A farmer is planning to grow tomatoes in a plot of size 200 ft by 500 ft. How much manure should he buy?
1. Area of the plot: 200 × 500 = 100000 square feet.
2. 1 acre is 43560 square feet, and 10 tonnes is 10000 kg.
3. 43560 : 10000 :: 100000 : x, so x = 10000 × 100000 ÷ 43560.
4. 10000 × 100000 ÷ 43560 ≈ 22956.8.
Answer: About 22956.8 kg of manure (about 23 tonnes)

content.text:
Figure it Out (unit conversions, question 10): One acre of land costs ₹1500000. What is the cost of 2400 square feet of the same land?
1. 1 acre is 43560 square feet.
2. 43560 : 1500000 :: 2400 : x.
3. x = 1500000 × 2400 ÷ 43560
4. 1500000 × 2400 ÷ 43560 ≈ 82645.
Answer: About ₹82645

content.text:
Ratios in the form of a : b indicate that for every 'a' unit of the first quantity, there are 'b' units of the second quantity. 'a' and 'b' are the terms in the ratio.
Two ratios, a : b and c : d, are proportional (written a : b :: c : d) if their terms change by the same factor, i.e., if ad = bc.
If x is divided into two parts in the ratio m : n, then the quantity of the first part is m × x/(m + n) and the quantity of the second part is n × x/(m + n).

content.text:
Binairo, also known as Takuzu, is a logic puzzle with simple rules. Binairo is generally played on a square grid with no particular size. Some cells start out filled with two symbols: here horizontal and vertical lines. The rest of the cells are empty. The task is to fill cells in such a way that:
Each row and each column must contain an equal number of horizontal and vertical lines.
More than two horizontal or vertical lines can't be adjacent.
Each row is unique. Each column is unique.
Solve the following Binairo puzzles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if a row already has two horizontal lines side by side, what must the next cell be?
2. Look for pairs first: a pair of the same symbol forces the other symbol on both sides.
3. Count next: once a row has half of one symbol, the rest must be the other.
4. Finally use uniqueness to separate rows or columns that would be the same.

content.text:
Worked example: In a Binairo row of 6 cells, the first two cells hold horizontal lines and the fifth holds a vertical line. Fill the row.
1. Two horizontal lines are adjacent, so the third cell must be a vertical line.
2. A row of 6 cells needs 3 of each symbol; so far there are 2 horizontal and 2 vertical.
3. The fourth cell next to a vertical pair would make three verticals if cells 3, 4 and 5 were all vertical, so cell 4 is horizontal.
4. That makes 3 horizontal lines, so cell 6 is vertical: H H V H V V.
Answer: H H V H V V
